newsitem.title: USA: Clinton talks campaign finance, Dole begins blitz.
newsitem.headline: Clinton talks campaign finance, Dole begins blitz.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, seeking to answer persistent questions about Democratic fundraising, planned to speak out during a Western campaign swing on Friday, as Bob Dole headed into a 96-hour marathon.

With his formerly commanding lead dipping into single digits in some opinion polls, Clinton was expected to defend his fundraising efforts even as he called for an overhaul of a campaign finance system that critics say invites influence-peddling.

"One thing he will suggest ... is that we need to reform those laws to minimise the kind of ... priority that has to be placed on fundraising," White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said in Santa Barbara, California, where Clinton began his campaign day.

Clinton has drawn withering attacks in the campaign's last week from Dole, the Republican challenger, and Reform Party candidate Ross Perot over Democratic fundraising methods, notably contributions from foreign individuals and businesses.

Questions about donations linked to interests in Indonesia and Taiwan have dogged Clinton's campaign, especially after senior Democratic fundraiser John Huang was suspended amid reports that he unlawfully solicited foreign contributions and had made dozens of visits to the White House since mid-1995.

As Clinton campaigned in California and the Southwest, Dole was gearing up for a round-the-clock last-ditch drive beginning at midday on Friday in Columbus, Ohio, and ending at midday on Nov. 5, Election Day. His itinerary calls for him to stay primarily in Middle America, including Michigan, Indiana, Kentucky, Nebraska, South Dakota and Colorado.
But Dole will also make forays into New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Nevada before winding up in California, seen as a Clinton stronghold but, with 54 electoral votes, the richest prize in the country.

Dole, 73, vowed to "give it all I got" in his uphill attempt to win the White House, with possible stops in 15 states with a total of 204 electoral votes. The winning candidate needs 270 electoral votes and most polls show Clinton with a commanding lead on this score.

Opinion polls measuring how likely voters will cast their ballots show the race narrowing, with the gap only 7.7 percentage points in Thursday's Reuters tracking poll. Clinton had earlier held leads of more than 20 points over Dole.

An indicator of the tightening race is Georgia, one of four Southern states Clinton carried in 1992. An opinion poll of 925 likely voters published on Friday in the Atlanta Journal-Constitution showed Clinton's lead in Georgia had dwindled to 3 points. He had led by 15 points a month ago.
